summary:
Indonesia's national framework applies in Jambi: an October 2025 presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto lists LGBTQ+ people and "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among nonmilitary threats to be monitored and controlled, alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, though reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Reporting indicates the maximum is two years' imprisonment; a separate source records one year, on complaint by an immediate family member.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; Jambi does not fall under them.

Enforcement elsewhere takes the form of venue raids against private gatherings. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena stated that the gathering violated no law. On 11 August 2025 three men were arrested over an LGBTQ community page on Facebook.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022; his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody. His mother alleges police beat him; Indonesian police deny that violence was used.

Vigilante violence against trans women is documented at national scale. Between 14 and 16 July 2026 mobs attacked trans women across Indonesia; in Bogor more than fifteen women were doused, stripped and beaten, with footage shared online. Reporting from August 2026 ties that wave to the government's framing of LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. Researchers describe anti-queer attitudes as markedly hardened since 2016, and a 2025 Pew survey found 93% of Indonesians regard homosexuality as morally unacceptable.

Legal gender recognition in Indonesia requires sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval, and LGBT people have no anti-discrimination protections under national law. Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025.

No Jambi-specific local ordinance, protection measure or documented incident was found in the audited sources. Visitors to Jambi are therefore governed by the national framework described above: official framing of LGBTQ+ visibility as subversive, selective prosecution under the adultery provision, and mob violence with weak accountability.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement texture differs sharply between provinces. Aceh and South Sumatra carry their own criminalising provisions, while Jambi has no sourced ordinance of its kind; the practical risk in Jambi is the national climate rather than a local statute.

Attitudinal data point in the same direction as the legal framing. A 2025 Pew survey found 93% of Indonesians regard homosexuality as morally unacceptable, and researchers document a marked hardening of anti-queer attitudes since 2016.

Indonesia's posture in international human rights bodies is consistent with the domestic framework: it voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025.

Private digital activity has produced arrests. The 11 August 2025 arrests over an LGBTQ Facebook community page indicate that online community-building carries exposure risk independent of physical venues.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition for Indonesian residents requires sex-reassignment surgery plus approval from a court; there is no administrative or self-declaration route.

Same-sex marriage is not available, so the 2 January 2026 adultery provision reaches consensual same-sex relations between adults. The provision can be activated on complaint by an immediate family member, which makes private disputes a route into criminal proceedings.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity under national law.

Residents and visitors in Aceh and South Sumatra are subject to provincial criminalising provisions that do not apply in Jambi; in Aceh, punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and were carried out publicly in February 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the penalty for the extra-marital sex offence: one records up to two years' imprisonment, another up to one year on complaint by an immediate family member. The operative figure is unresolved in the audited inventory.

No Jambi-specific finding was located: the inventory contains no local ordinance, no protection measure and no documented incident for Jambi, and one source dedicated to Jambi produced no usable finding. Whether Jambi has enacted any morality or public-order ordinance with bearing on trans people is not sourced either way.

The 14-16 July 2026 vigilante wave and the 2022 death in custody are sourced to national reporting; neither is attributed to Jambi, and the death rests on an allegation by the family that police deny.

The 93% figure comes from a 2025 Pew survey whose Jambi-level breakdown is not in the inventory.
